description:
The Mumbai Heritage Walk is a great way to experience the city’s vibrant culture and rich history.
Mumbai Heritage Walk is probably known as the ‘dream city’ and rightly so the city is indeed like a beautiful, magnificent dream. Old Mumbai is the part of Mumbai that represents its heritage and history. Reflecting on the time of Colonial era, the area is studded with numerous tourist attractions. From Chhatrapati Shivaji terminus to the ‘White town’ to the University library to the magnificent Marine drive, the city has so many spectacular attractions that one can never miss. Explore all these places of Old Mumbai and many more with this heritage walk tour.

Walking tours expose many residents and visitors to the structures.

featured_reviews.review_text: Arpan was great- he was very knowledgeable about the history of India and of the places he took us. He began by providing us with context for everywhere we were going to go that day, showing us on a map what the route would look like and why he chose the places he was taking us to. featured_reviews.name: Derishta Pillay
featured_reviews.review_text:
At the outset I must say that neither myself nor my husband are huge fans of the usual guided walking tours mainly because we hate being taken to cliched and crowded tourist hotspots, listening to facts straight from the Wikipedia page and jostling for space with other tourists just to return sunburned and underwhelmed. In addition we'd already spent a hectic 5 weeks in India - we were tired, grumpy, waiting to fly back home and not at all looking forward to our last 4 days in Mumbai at all. So basically when our travel companions insisted we book a tour - the scene was set for disaster...
'Bombay Walks' single handedly turned this around and Mumbai actually turned out to be the highlight of our trip! (Nope this is not a sponsored review 😂)

The tour: Arpan's tour extends to the days before and after the actual tour as he offers valuable advice about where to stay/eat/party/shop etc. He speaks perfect English, is pleasant and very easy to communicate with. His passion and love for the city is infectious and you will end his tour enthralled, overwhelmed and completely charmed by Mumbai and it's people - vowing to come back and dig deeper, spend longer and see more. The city tour covers many facets of the city - traveling to hidden gems and local landmarks across the length and breadth of Mumbai. You get to see and experience aspects of Mumbai that you'd never be able to do alone with a guide book or google maps - like traveling on local trains and walking through Worli fishing village and stopping by at small off-the-beaten path temples and churches.

The guide: Arpan is reliable, trustworthy and comes well prepared for the type of group. His talking style is light-hearted and easy going but still knowledgeable and always engaging. He's the type of guide that can tell you interesting facts about the history, architecture and politics of a place but also where to get the best coconut water along the way and which public toilets are ok to use.
We only met Arpan in person on the day of the tour and although we were constantly bombarded with sights, sounds and smells (it is Mumbai after all) - it never once felt like we were just being dragged from point to point whilst he rattled off information but rather that we were spending the day walking around with an old friend.

Target travelers: We're fairly well travelled and yet this is the first time we've ever bothered to leave a tour review - on any platform - I think that in itself indicates how highly we recommend this tour.
This is really a 'must do' in Mumbai.
It's so good we would do this tour again even if it were to cover the exact route we already took. The walking wasn't particular strenuous so it's recommended for any age group it should also be noted that we found that     Arpan was discreetly always conscious of where the group members were and their safety and constantly aware of our surroundings and the locals around us - on that note I would recommend this tour even if you're a single female traveling alone.

When to do it: Try and do this tour on your first full day in Mumbai because it's also a great way to orientate yourself around the city and plan the rest of your time there.

That city that everyone talks about - that's all of India's many faces and layers in one, that accepts everyone, that's everyone's home - regardless of language, religion or creed - Mumbai is THAT city and you'd be crazy if you miss the opportunity to let a born-and-bred local guide you around...

featured_reviews.name: Moni K.

featured_reviews.review_text:

featured_reviews.name: Birgitte Copmann
featured_reviews.review_text:
Mumbai is a big mouthful that needs to be taken in small bites.
We, a Danish couple, were lucky to have a whole day with two highly qualified guides.
The first part was the classic highlights of Mumbai, but thanks to Muhammed's in-depth knowledge of the city we got a lot more that is not described in the guide books. It was historical as well as social,  and places of cultural importance.
The day ended with a local guide in the slum of Dharavi. Very overwhelming and very different from what we had imagined. Here we were shown small businesses, leather, textiles - and an effective way to recycle plastic. We saw happy faces in the very narrow alleys, children playing and hardworking people who cope with life's challenges despite the lack of comfort and non-existent luxury.
Our dedicated guides Mohammed and Ahmed took us on a journey into a very foreign culture, giving us understanding and perspective on the megacity of Mumbai

featured_reviews.name: Х. У. З.
featured_reviews.review_text: I called to book my tour the same morning and was happy that they were able to accommodate me last minute! Aamir was my guide for the slum and laundry tour - he clearly knew where he was going and what he was doing, and although I could tell he had walked the same route many times before, it didn’t feel touristy or artificial at all. It just felt like we were walking through a neighborhood he knew well, where more or less everything was open to the outside world. We started off in the area where there are many small factories for clothing, recycling, and bakery products - at every little business we encountered, he simply had to ask to enter, and we could walk right in and see the process up close. It was fascinating to me - I never would have imagined that the bread I buy in a supermarket or clothes I buy in a normal store come from such small-scale operations and not major, industrial manufacturing plants. We also passed through a residential area, and I even stopped to get henna done from a woman we met at random while inside her neighbor’s pottery studio. For that reason, we didn’t have a lot of time towards the end, and the laundry was just a stopover at the lookout over the area (where I was mobbed by vendors trying to sell me things; an expected part of being an outsider in India), but overall it felt like a very authentic look into the everyday lives of much of Mumbai’s lower class. I took a private tour so I wasn’t in a big group, and I’m not that much into taking photos so we moved very fast - which is what I preferred as there was so much to see. Highly recommended.

featured_reviews.name: Kailash
featured_reviews.review_text:
Sewri Fort in Mumbai is a captivating historical landmark that offers a glimpse into the city's rich past. With its intriguing architecture and serene surroundings, it is a must-visit destination for history enthusiasts and explorers alike.

The fort's age-old stone walls exude a sense of grandeur, evoking memories of its colonial and maritime significance. As you wander through the ruins, you'll be transported back in time to an era when the fort played a crucial role in safeguarding the city against potential invaders.

The location of Sewri Fort adds to its charm. Situated along the eastern waterfront of Mumbai, it provides a stunning panoramic view of the sea and mangroves, making it a delightful spot for photography and relaxation.

Though the fort is in ruins, the Maharashtra Government has taken measures to preserve its heritage, adding information boards that share historical anecdotes. The fort's simplicity and lack of commercialization add to its allure, allowing visitors to soak in the authentic essence of Mumbai's history.

However, it is essential to note that the site lacks amenities and can be challenging to access for people with mobility issues due to uneven terrain. Nevertheless, the overall experience of visiting Sewri Fort is rewarding and educational, offering a memorable journey through Mumbai's past.

Mumbai is blessed with so many forts strategically located at it's coast line like Worli Fort, Mazagoan Fort, Madh Fort, Bandra Fort, Mahim Fort and Sewri Fort. Amongst all these forts I think Bandra Fort and Sewri Fort are decently taken care by the authorities. Sewri Fort is just about 1-2km distance from Sewri station. It's strategic location is such that you can enjoy sunrise ⛅ if you go early on the morning. A beautiful red sun coming out of Creek water presents magnificent view. Fort is relatively in good shape though it's not a very big fort but it's structure is very much intact. At one side of the fort is a huge Creek from where you can see classic Flamingo point where thousands of flamingo migrates every year to this place and from the other side of the fort you can see highrise buildings of Mumbai. There is also a Durga near to this fort with good number of huge trees around presenting a nice view soothing to the eyes.

There is no security guards taking care of this fort and there is no entry fees also. We reached to this place on our cycles and found approach road in a good condition. If you visit to this Fort, don't forget to visit Flamingo point also which is half a km from this place. Don't expect too much from this place but you won't b disappointed if you visit this place.

Hope you will find my review useful. I recommend you to discover this hidden and unknown place of Mumbai and spread a word so more n more people visits this place and authorities awakes to take good care of this fort.

featured_reviews.name: TheR Side
featured_reviews.review_text:
Visiting Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus is not just about seeing a railway station — it feels like witnessing a living piece of Indian history. This iconic landmark of Mumbai is one of the most beautiful railway stations in the world and a proud symbol of India’s architectural heritage. Built in 1887 during the British era to celebrate Queen Victoria’s Golden Jubilee, the station was originally known as Victoria Terminus (VT). Later, it was renamed in honor of the great Maratha king Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj.

The architecture of CSMT is truly breathtaking. Designed by British architect Frederick William Stevens, the building is a perfect blend of Victorian Gothic Revival style and traditional Indian architecture. Every corner of the station showcases detailed stone carvings, massive domes, pointed arches, stained glass windows, wooden ceilings, iron structures, and artistic statues. The central dome with the statue holding a torch represents progress and development. Even after more than a century, the structure still looks grand and royal.

What makes this place truly special is that it is not just a railway station — it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Mumbai’s greatest identities. Millions of people travel through this station every day, making it one of the busiest railway stations in India. Yet beyond the crowd and trains, CSMT stands as a symbol of Mumbai’s spirit, history, culture, and nonstop energy. The station has appeared in many Bollywood movies, documentaries, and photographs because of its iconic beauty and historic importance.

The construction itself was considered an engineering masterpiece of its time. Huge stones were brought from different places, and skilled Indian craftsmen worked for years on the carvings and decorations. The building combines advanced British engineering with Indian artistic craftsmanship, which is why it still stands strong today. At night, when the entire structure lights up, it looks absolutely magical and royal.

Whether you love history, photography, architecture, or travel, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus is a place everyone should experience at least once. It is not just a station where trains arrive and depart — it is the heartbeat of Mumbai, a masterpiece of art and engineering, and a timeless monument that tells the story of India’s colonial past and modern progress together.

The station is well-connected and always full of energy, showcasing the true spirit of Mumbai. Watching the constant movement of people and trains adds to its unique charm.
However, like most busy stations, it can get very crowded, especially during peak hours, which may feel overwhelming for some visitors.
Overall, a must-visit place for its historical significance and architectural beauty.

featured_reviews.review_text:
CSMT is one of the best connected railway stations in Mumbai and a perfect base if you want to explore the city. The station itself is a UNESCO World Heritage Site – beautiful old architecture, huge space and a constant buzzing vibe.

What makes CSMT amazing is how close it is to most major tourist spots in South Mumbai. Within 10–20 minutes you can reach places like Gateway of India, Marine Drive, Colaba Causeway, Crawford Market, Girgaon Chowpatty, Haji Ali, Worli Sea Face and many more. Taxis, buses and even metro connectivity are easily available right outside the station.

It also connects very smoothly to other major stations like Byculla, Dadar, Kurla, Wadala Road, Sewri, Sandhurst Road and gives quick access to both Central and Harbour lines. Plenty of food options, ATMs, luggage areas and local shops are available inside and around the station.

If you’re visiting Mumbai or planning a quick day trip around South Mumbai, starting from CSMT makes everything super convenient. Safe, historic, well-connected and surrounded by most of the city’s iconic locations.

Visited Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT) in 2026 and observed the station mainly from the outside. The building continues to be one of Mumbai’s most iconic landmarks, with its stunning Victorian Gothic architecture standing out beautifully, especially during the evening when it is well-lit. The structure is well-maintained and gives a grand, historic vibe that reflects the city’s heritage.

However, the surrounding area outside the station is quite busy and chaotic, which is expected given its central location. There is constant movement of taxis, buses, and local commuters, making the area crowded throughout the day. While the roads are functional, traffic management could still be improved to reduce congestion and make pedestrian movement smoother.

Cleanliness outside the station is decent but not consistent. Certain areas are maintained well, while some corners still need better upkeep and regular cleaning. The presence of street vendors adds to the local experience, but at times it contributes to crowding and slight clutter around entry points.

Security presence is visible, and there are barricades and checkpoints that help manage the flow of people. Lighting at night is a big plus, making the area feel relatively safe and visually appealing.

Overall, the outside view of CSMT is a mix of heritage beauty and typical Mumbai hustle. It’s a must-visit spot for its architecture and vibe, but improvements in cleanliness and crowd management would make the experience much better.

Hutatma Chowk is located in the busy financial district of Fort. It derives its present name from an incident in 1956 when a peaceful demonstration by the Samyukta Maharashtra Samiti (United Maharashtra Committee) was fired upon by the police resulting in 106 deaths. The incident was part of ongoing struggles of the Samyukta Maharashtra Samiti, amongst others, for the creation of the State of Maharashtra. The shooting proved to be a major impetus for the creation of Maharashtra on 1 May 1960.

The Hutatma Chowk square is lined on all sides by buildings constructed during the British Raj. An ornate fountain surrounded by delicately carved figures forms the center of the huge square. This was the Flora Fountain.

The fountain itself was built in 1864 and represents the Roman Goddess Flora, the Goddess of Abundance. Today, it is a heritage structure. It cost Rs. 47,000 to build, a large sum at the time, and was constructed by the Agri-Horticultural Society of Western India. Cursetjee Fardoonjee Parekh donated Rs.20,000 towards the construction of this fountain. The fountain was carved from stone that was imported from Portland. It was built in honour of Sir Bartle Frere, who was the Governor of Bombay at the time. Sir Bartle was responsible for dismantling Bombay Fort and shaping much of modern Mumbai. Initially it was to be named after the Governor but the name was changed before the fountain was unveiled. When it was constructed, it was in the middle of the city. Flora fountain stands in exactly the same place where the original Churchgate of Bombay Fort stood. The area around Flora Fountain is the business center of Mumbai and is surrounded by offices, banks, colleges and shops.

This is usually part of stops during heritage walks.

Today it is located between Union Bank of India on one side & Punjab National Bank on the other. Not sure if the clock works though as it seems to be stuck on ten to six.

An unusual and interesting clock tower.
